overview.intro: The German collapse into dictatorship between 1933 and 1939 destroyed the Weimar Republic, remilitarised German society and ended the European settlement of 1919 by force. This unit covers the weaknesses of the Weimar Republic, the growth and ideology of the Nazi party, the appointment of Hitler as chancellor and the establishment of a one-party state, the methods by which the regime secured control of society, the remilitarisation of the Rhineland and the events of 1938, and the origins of the Second World War.

learningOutcomes: Describe the weaknesses of the Weimar Republic.
Explain the growth and the ideology of the Nazi party.

Explain the remilitarisation of the Rhineland, the Anschluss and Munich, and the outbreak of war.

learn.title: The Weimar Republic and its weaknesses

blocks.text: The Weimar Constitution of 1919 created a republic with universal suffrage including women, a directly elected president and a Reichstag elected by proportional representation. Proportional representation gave seats to parties in exact proportion to their votes, which produced a parliament of many small parties and made a stable coalition difficult to hold. Article 48 allowed the president to rule by emergency decree when public security was disturbed, a power used repeatedly in the final years of the republic and which eventually provided the constitutional cover for the dictatorship itself.

The republic also carried burdens it had not created. It was associated from the start with the armistice and the Treaty of Versailles, and the myth that the army had been stabbed in the back rather than defeated gave its enemies a permanent argument. The reparations crisis of 1923 brought hyperinflation that wiped out the savings of the middle class, and the depression after 1929 brought unemployment beyond anything the constitutional parties could answer. The parties of the left were divided between social democrats and communists, who followed Moscow in treating the social democrats as their principal enemy, while the parties of the centre and right spent the last years of the republic in presidential government rather than parliamentary majorities.

learn.title: The Nazi party and its ideology

blocks.text: The party was founded in 1920 as the German Workers’ Party and renamed by Hitler, who joined its early meetings as an army informer and soon became its principal speaker. Its twenty-five point programme of 1920 combined nationalist slogans with attacks on the peace settlement, on Jewish financiers and on the privileges of capital, a mixture designed to draw votes from across the resentments of the post-war years. The party’s growth was interrupted by the failed beer hall putsch of November 1923, after which Hitler was imprisoned, dictated Mein Kampf and resolved to take power by legal means.

The ideology rested on racial hierarchy, with the German people presented as the master race, antisemitism as a central doctrine rather than an incidental prejudice, contempt for democracy as a foreign and weak system, and the destruction of the Versailles settlement with the recovery of lost territory and colonies. The party built an appeal that was deliberately vague on economics while being precise on nation and race, and it organised an entire parallel culture through the SA, the Hitler Youth, women’s and professional associations, so that a member had somewhere to belong at every hour of the week.

learn.title: Seizure of power and the one-party state

blocks.text: Hitler was appointed chancellor on 30 January 1933 in a cabinet that contained only two other Nazis, through a deal by conservative politicians who believed they could control him. The Reichstag fire of 27 February 1933 was used to suspend civil liberties, and the decree for the protection of people and state allowed arrests without trial. In the election of March 1933, held with the communists banned and the SA deployed, the Nazis won 44 per cent, still short of a majority, and on 23 March the Enabling Act was passed with the support of the centre parties, which permitted the cabinet to make laws without parliament for four years.

Within months the state was a one-party system. Communist and then socialist deputies were arrested or fled, other parties dissolved themselves or were banned, trade unions were abolished on 2 May 1933 and their assets seized, and the concordat with the Vatican in July gave international recognition to the regime while it removed a potential source of opposition. In June 1934 the Night of the Long Knives destroyed the leadership of the SA, which reassured the army that its position was secure, and when Hindenburg died in August 1934 the offices of president and chancellor were combined in Hitler’s person, with the armed forces swearing a personal oath to him.

learn.title: Control of society and the road to war

blocks.text: Control was built through several reinforcing institutions. The Gestapo secret police and the SD monitored opposition, the courts were brought into line and special tribunals allowed punishment without ordinary procedure, censorship controlled the press and book burning was staged in 1933, and the radio was made cheap enough to be in every household so that the regime spoke directly into it. indoctrination worked through the education system and the Hitler Youth, which reached almost every young person, while the propaganda ministry under Goebbels coordinated message and spectacle. Terror operated alongside consent: the regime was popular for much of the period because rearmament and public works ended unemployment, because VW and other promises improved living standards, and because the successes abroad were presented as the recovery of national honour.

Foreign policy dismantled the settlement of 1919 step by step. Rearmament began openly with the reintroduction of conscription in 1935, the Rhineland was remilitarised in March 1936 in violation of the treaties, and Austria was annexed in March 1938 through the Anschluss. At Munich in September 1938 Britain and France agreed to the cession of the Sudetenland, and the agreement was presented as peace for our time, but Germany took the rest of the Czech lands in March 1939. The occupation of Prague finally destroyed the policy of appeasement, and after Germany demanded Danzig and the Polish corridor, Britain and France guaranteed Poland’s independence. Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, and Britain and France declared war on 3 September.

questions.explanation: He was appointed by President Hindenburg in a coalition cabinet that contained only two other Nazis.

questions.prompt: The German constitution of 1919 that established the republic is known as the Weimar __________ .
questions.explanation: It provided universal suffrage, proportional representation and the emergency powers of article 48.

questions.prompt: The purge of June 1934 in which the SA leadership was destroyed is known as the Night of the Long __________ .
questions.explanation: It reassured the army that its position was secure and removed a rival power centre.

questions.prompt: State four weaknesses of the Weimar Republic.
questions.answer: Four weaknesses are: proportional representation, which produced many small parties and unstable coalitions; the emergency powers of article 48, which normalised rule by decree before 1933; the association of the republic with the Treaty of Versailles and the armistice, which exposed it to the charge of betrayal; and the economic crises of hyperinflation in 1923 and mass unemployment after 1929, which destroyed confidence in the democratic parties. The division of the left between social democrats and communists is also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each weakness must be explained as a mechanism that weakened republican government.

questions.prompt: Explain how the Nazis established a one-party state in 1933.
questions.answer: The process began with the decree for the protection of people and state, issued after the Reichstag fire of 27 February 1933, which suspended civil liberties and allowed arrest without trial. In the election of March, held with communist candidates banned and the SA deployed, the Nazis won 44 per cent, which was still short of a majority, so on 23 March the Enabling Act was passed with the support of the centre parties and allowed the cabinet to make laws without parliament. Communist deputies were arrested or fled, socialist deputies were removed under the protective custody powers, and the remaining parties were either persuaded to dissolve or banned, so by mid-1933 no legal opposition existed. The trade unions were abolished on 2 May 1933 and their funds seized, removing the organisation of the working class. Finally the Night of the Long Knives in June 1934 destroyed the SA leadership and secured the army, and after Hindenburg’s death in August the offices of president and chancellor were combined in Hitler’s person, with the armed forces swearing a personal oath to him.
questions.explanation: The answer needs the sequence from emergency decree through Enabling Act to party, union and presidential consolidation.

questions.prompt: Explain how the Nazi regime secured control of German society, and assess its popularity.
questions.answer: Control combined institutions of repression with institutions of consent. The Gestapo and the SD monitored opinion and could arrest without procedure, special tribunals removed the protection of ordinary courts, the press was censored, books were burned in 1933, and the propaganda ministry under Goebbels coordinated message, spectacle and the calendar of public events. The radio was produced cheaply enough to be present in every household, which allowed the regime to speak directly into it. Education and the Hitler Youth worked on the young, while the Labour Front replaced independent unions and thereby removed the worker’s independent organisation. Against this, popularity was genuine in substantial parts of the population for much of the period: the regime ended mass unemployment through rearmament and public works such as the autobahns, the Volkswagen promise and the strength through joy programme improved leisure and living standards, the churches were pacified through the concordat of 1933, and the diplomatic successes of 1935 to 1938 were presented as the recovery of national honour. The assessment should therefore avoid both extremes: terror made opposition extremely dangerous and therefore invisible, which exaggerates apparent consent, while material benefit and nationalism produced support that no amount of terror alone could have created. The combination, rather than either element alone, explains the regime’s grip.
questions.explanation: Full marks need named institutions for control, specific measures that produced consent, and an explicit judgement on how far consent was real.

questions.prompt: Was the outbreak of the Second World War the result of Nazi aggression or of the failures of the other European powers?
questions.answer: The case for Nazi aggression rests on a clear sequence of violations, each initiated by Germany: rearmament and the reintroduction of conscription in 1935, the remilitarisation of the Rhineland in 1936 against treaty obligations, the annexation of Austria in 1938, the demand for and seizure of the Sudetenland at Munich, the occupation of the Czech lands in March 1939 and the invasion of Poland in September. Each step was a decision taken by the German government to overturn the settlement by force, and Hitler’s own writing in Mein Kampf had specified the objectives of territory in the east years before. The case for the failures of the other powers is also substantial. France and Britain accepted the Anschluss, gave away the Sudetenland at Munich on the assumption that German claims could be satisfied, failed to enforce the disarmament clauses when Germany was weakest in 1935–36, and allowed the Rhineland to be reoccupied without response at a moment when the German army was too slight to resist. The failure of the League over Abyssinia and Manchuria had already shown that collective security would not be enforced, and the Soviet Pact of August 1939 removed the last deterrent on Germany’s eastern border. The most defensible judgement assigns responsibility in two parts: the war was caused by a policy of deliberate expansion that a stronger and more united response might have checked at several points before 1939, and it was the cumulative failure of that response that made the final act possible without earlier opposition. An answer that gives only one side should still be argued from evidence, but the stronger answer shows that aggression explains the direction and failures explain the timing.
questions.explanation: Full marks require a dated sequence of German acts, a parallel sequence of western responses and a judgement that separates cause of direction from cause of opportunity.
